yield-curve-10y2y.oneLine: The gap between long and short-term US government borrowing.
yield-curve-10y2y.ifRising: A widening gap usually comes with growth or inflation pressure.
yield-curve-10y2y.ifFalling: A small or negative gap has preceded most US recessions.

connections.text: Both read the same recession signal from different angles.

yield-curve-10y3m.oneLine: The gap the Federal Reserve itself watches most closely.
yield-curve-10y3m.ifRising: A steep gap usually comes with growth or inflation pressure.
yield-curve-10y3m.ifFalling: Deep inversions of this leg have preceded every modern US recession.

connections.text: The 3-month leg and the recession model tell the same story.

real-yield-10y.oneLine: What lending to the US government pays after inflation is taken out.
real-yield-10y.ifRising: Safe savings pay more, so assets that pay no interest, like gold, often get less attractive.
real-yield-10y.ifFalling: Holding safe money earns little after inflation, which often helps non-interest assets.

connections.text: Higher real yields tend to weigh on gold.

real-yield-10y.australiaAngle: High US real yields tend to pressure the Australian dollar and gold prices.

us10y.oneLine: The interest rate on 10-year US government debt.
us10y.ifRising: Home loans and business credit usually follow, with a lag.
us10y.ifFalling: Cheaper borrowing usually helps loans and asset prices.

connections.text: The 30-year US mortgage follows the 10-year Treasury.
The nominal yield is roughly the real yield plus expected inflation.

us10y.australiaAngle: Australian long-term rates and the Australian dollar usually move with US long yields.

us30y.oneLine: The interest rate on 30-year US government debt.
us30y.ifRising: Mortgages and long-dated borrowing usually cost more.

connections.text: The 30-year Treasury is the longest anchor for US mortgage pricing.

fed-target.oneLine: The Federal Reserve’s main interest rate.
fed-target.ifRising: Loans and mortgages usually cost more, and saving pays more.
fed-target.ifFalling: Loans and mortgages usually ease, and saving pays less.

connections.text: The policy rate anchors the short end; the 10-year carries the long expectation.

fed-target.australiaAngle: The Fed’s moves set the tone for global rates, including the path the RBA can credibly take.

ecb-dfr.oneLine: The rate banks earn on deposits at the European Central Bank.
ecb-dfr.ifRising: Euro-area loans usually cost more, and saving pays more.
ecb-dfr.ifFalling: Euro-area loans usually ease, and saving pays less.

connections.text: The deposit rate anchors the short end of the euro-area curve.

fed-expectations.plainName: Where markets think the Fed goes
fed-expectations.oneLine: What the 2-year Treasury implies about the Fed’s next moves.
fed-expectations.ifRising: When markets price higher Fed rates, borrowing usually rises before the move.
fed-expectations.ifFalling: When markets price lower Fed rates, borrowing usually eases before the move.

connections.text: The 2-year-implied path is the market’s reading of where the Fed goes.

govt-interest-revenue.oneLine: How big the US government’s interest bill on its debt is, versus its income.
govt-interest-revenue.ifRising: More tax money usually goes to interest payments, sharpening fights over the US budget.
govt-interest-revenue.ifFalling: A smaller interest slice usually leaves more room for other government spending.

connections.text: Higher long-term rates raise the interest the government pays over time.

us-2y.oneLine: The interest rate on 2-year US government debt.
us-2y.ifRising: Markets usually expect higher Fed rates, and near-term borrowing costs often follow.
us-2y.ifFalling: Markets usually expect lower Fed rates, bringing earlier relief for borrowers.

connections.text: The market-expectations card is built from this 2-year rate.
This is the short leg of the 10-year-minus-2-year gap.

sofr.oneLine: What banks actually pay to borrow cash overnight in the US.
sofr.ifRising: Loans whose rate moves daily usually get more expensive.
sofr.ifFalling: Short-term borrowing usually gets cheaper, taking pressure off borrowers.

connections.text: SOFR normally sits just under the top of the Fed’s target range.

mortgage-30y.oneLine: The average rate on a new 30-year US home loan.
mortgage-30y.ifRising: Monthly payments on new home loans usually rise, and fewer buyers can afford them.
mortgage-30y.ifFalling: New home loans usually get cheaper, letting buyers borrow a little more.

connections.text: The 30-year mortgage follows the 10-year Treasury rate.
Policy moves reach this rate through the long end, with a delay.

jgb-10y.oneLine: The interest rate on 10-year Japanese government debt.
jgb-10y.ifRising: Japanese money usually gets tighter at home, and world markets often feel it.
jgb-10y.ifFalling: Cheap Japanese money usually stays available for borrowers and world markets.

connections.text: The US-Japan 10-year gap card is built from this rate.
The Bank of Japan still leans heavily on this market.

bund-10y.oneLine: The interest rate on 10-year German government debt.
bund-10y.ifRising: Borrowing across Europe usually gets more expensive, from mortgages to business loans.
bund-10y.ifFalling: Borrowing across Europe usually eases, from home loans to business credit.

connections.text: The daily euro safe-rate and this monthly German mirror tell one story.
The ECB’s policy rate anchors the base this long-term rate floats above.

gilt-10y.oneLine: The interest rate on 10-year UK government debt.
gilt-10y.ifRising: UK mortgages and business loans usually get more expensive.
gilt-10y.ifFalling: UK borrowing usually gets cheaper, helping loans and house prices.

connections.text: The Bank of England sets the short base; this is the market’s long rate.

euro-aaa-10y.oneLine: The 10-year borrowing cost of the euro area’s safest governments.
euro-aaa-10y.ifRising: Safe long-term rates in Europe usually rise with it, making loans dearer.
euro-aaa-10y.ifFalling: Cheap safe money in Europe usually eases loans and asset prices.

connections.text: The ECB’s policy rate anchors the short end; this is the safe long end.
The German mirror tells the same story with a monthly delay.

boe-rate.oneLine: The Bank of England’s main interest rate.
boe-rate.ifRising: UK loans and mortgages usually cost more, and saving pays more.
boe-rate.ifFalling: UK borrowing usually eases and saving pays less.

connections.text: The Bank sets the short rate; gilts carry the long one.

boj-rate.oneLine: The Bank of Japan’s main interest rate.
boj-rate.ifRising: Cheap Japanese money usually pulls back home, shaking world markets at times.
boj-rate.ifFalling: Cheap Japanese money usually stays easy fuel for world borrowing.

connections.text: The Bank of Japan’s setting steers the 10-year bond market heavily.
The yen’s value moves with what Japan’s central bank does.

dollar-basket.oneLine: The US dollar measured against a group of six big currencies.
dollar-basket.ifRising: A stronger dollar often pressures world prices, debts and other currencies.
dollar-basket.ifFalling: A weaker dollar usually eases pressure on world trade and debts.

connections.text: A stronger dollar often weighs on gold prices.
The euro is the biggest weight inside the basket.

dollar-basket.australiaAngle: A stronger US dollar usually weighs on the Australian dollar and on commodity prices.

usdjpy.oneLine: How many Japanese yen one US dollar buys.
usdjpy.ifRising: Japanese goods and travel usually get cheaper for people paying in other currencies.
usdjpy.ifFalling: A rising yen often means worry, as money borrowed in yen moves home fast.

connections.text: The US-Japan rate gap is the reward that keeps the yen carry trade alive.
The Bank of Japan’s rate is the yen’s home base.

usdjpy.australiaAngle: When the yen surges on worry, the Australian dollar often sags with other risk currencies.

us-japan-10y-gap.oneLine: How much more the US pays to borrow for 10 years than Japan.
us-japan-10y-gap.ifRising: The reward for borrowing cheap Japanese money to earn US rates usually grows.
us-japan-10y-gap.ifFalling: The cheap-yen trade pays less, and its retreat can shake world markets.

connections.text: Dollar-yen is the trade; this gap is its fuel line.
The US side of the gap is the 10-year Treasury rate.
The Japan side is the 10-year Japanese government bond.

us-japan-10y-gap.australiaAngle: When this gap narrows fast, the Australian dollar often weakens with other carry favorites.

eur-usd.oneLine: How many euros one US dollar buys.
eur-usd.ifRising: A stronger dollar against the euro often pressures world prices.
eur-usd.ifFalling: A weaker dollar usually eases pressure on world prices and trade.

connections.text: The euro is the biggest single weight in the dollar basket.
The Fed steers the dollar’s side; the ECB steers the euro’s.

usdtry.oneLine: How many Turkish liras one US dollar buys.
usdtry.ifRising: Imported goods in Turkey usually get dearer as the lira slides.
usdtry.ifFalling: A firmer lira usually means calmer inflation and a rare stretch of stability.

connections.text: Turkey sits outside the big-currency basket, but lira trouble often comes with a strong dollar.

usdaed.oneLine: How many UAE dirhams one US dollar buys.
usdaed.ifRising: The dirham’s dollar peg usually absorbs this: the pair barely moves by design.
usdaed.ifFalling: A meaningful drop would be an exceptional event: the peg has held for decades.

connections.text: The dirham is pegged TO the dollar, so it moves with it against every other currency.
Gulf economies ride oil income; the peg keeps that income dollar-linked.

us-unemployment.oneLine: The share of the US workforce without a job.
us-unemployment.ifRising: A steady climb usually means the US economy is cooling, and pay rises soften.
us-unemployment.ifFalling: Falling joblessness usually comes with a strong jobs market and steadier pay growth.

connections.text: The recession alarm beside this card is built from this rate.
Jobs added and the jobless rate come from the same monthly report.

sahm-rule.oneLine: An alarm built from US joblessness that rings when a downturn has usually begun.
sahm-rule.ifRising: A fast rise in joblessness usually means a downturn has already started.
sahm-rule.ifFalling: A falling reading usually means the jobs market is out of alarm territory.

connections.text: The alarm watches this rate’s climb from its recent low.
The model and the alarm read the same downturn from different angles.

china-pmi.oneLine: A monthly survey of factory managers in China.
china-pmi.ifRising: Chinese factories are usually getting busier, often good news for world trade.
china-pmi.ifFalling: Chinese factories are usually slowing, which often weighs on world trade and commodity prices.

connections.text: Read the factory pulse beside China’s price gauge to judge its demand.
Copper often moves with Chinese factory strength.

china-cpi.oneLine: How fast consumer prices in China are rising, versus a year ago.
china-cpi.ifRising: Overheating pressure in the world’s factory often builds, rippling into world goods prices.
china-cpi.ifFalling: Weak Chinese demand usually drags on world trade and commodity prices.

connections.text: The factory pulse and the price gauge together judge Chinese demand.

copper-gold.ifRising: Markets are usually paying up for growth signals, like factory building.
copper-gold.ifFalling: Money usually shifts toward safe havens, a mix that often comes with world slowdowns.

connections.text: Copper is the growth leg of this measure.
Gold is the safety leg.

michigan-sentiment.oneLine: How confident American households feel about their money.
michigan-sentiment.ifRising: Confident households usually keep spending, which supports the economy.
michigan-sentiment.ifFalling: Gloomy households usually cut back on spending first.

connections.text: The price-worry number rides inside this survey.
Mood often leads actual spending.

initial-jobless-claims.oneLine: How many Americans newly filed for jobless benefits last week.
initial-jobless-claims.ifRising: Layoffs are usually picking up, the earliest sign of a softening jobs market.
initial-jobless-claims.ifFalling: Layoffs are usually rare, a sign of a tight jobs market.

connections.text: Weekly claims feed the monthly jobless rate.
Claim surges arrive long before this alarm can ring.

philly-fed.oneLine: An early monthly read on US factory activity.
philly-fed.ifRising: More US manufacturers are usually growing, an early sign of strength.
philly-fed.ifFalling: More US manufacturers are usually shrinking, an early sign of weakness.

connections.text: Factory surveys often turn before the headline growth number.

recession-probability.oneLine: A model’s estimate of the chance the US economy is in a downturn.
recession-probability.ifRising: The data looks more and more like past downturns, though models trail the real economy.
recession-probability.ifFalling: The data reads more and more like normal expansion.

connections.text: The alarm and the model read the same downturn from different angles.
The model weighs many inputs, growth among them, and publishes with a lag.

oecd-cli-us.oneLine: A gauge that usually turns before the whole US economy does.
oecd-cli-us.ifRising: The US economy’s direction is usually improving several months out.
oecd-cli-us.ifFalling: A US slowdown usually sits several months ahead.

connections.text: Read the early gauge beside the recession odds.
The claims number confirms turns much faster.

m2-us.oneLine: The total money sitting in US bank accounts and wallets.
m2-us.ifRising: Spending power usually builds, which can feed inflation later.
m2-us.ifFalling: Rare shrinkage that has historically clustered around US downturns.

connections.text: Money growth is one input in inflation debates.
The central bank’s own balance sheet is one engine behind it.

retail-sales.oneLine: The monthly value of what American shops ring up.
retail-sales.ifRising: Consumer spending is usually carrying the economy.
retail-sales.ifFalling: A spending pullback usually opens the door to recession talk.

connections.text: Mood often leads this spending number.
Spending is most of the US economy.

housing-permits.oneLine: How many new US homes were cleared to start this month.
housing-permits.ifRising: Builders usually expect enough demand to justify new homes.
housing-permits.ifFalling: Builders usually shelve projects, a classic early response to expensive borrowing.

connections.text: Permits are the market’s answer to the mortgage rate.

job-openings.oneLine: How many unfilled jobs US employers are trying to fill.
job-openings.ifRising: Employers usually still want workers, a sign of labour demand.
job-openings.ifFalling: Hiring appetite usually fades before joblessness rises.

connections.text: Openings usually turn before the jobless rate does.
One counts employers pulling back; the other workers being let go.

us-gdp-growth.oneLine: How much bigger the US economy got last quarter.
us-gdp-growth.ifRising: A faster US economy usually keeps world rates higher for longer.
us-gdp-growth.ifFalling: Weak US growth usually brings rate-cut hopes and recession talk.

connections.text: Spending is most of the economy this number measures.
Jobs and growth usually move together.

us-nfp.oneLine: How many jobs America added or lost last month.
us-nfp.ifRising: Strong hiring usually keeps world interest rates higher.
us-nfp.ifFalling: Job losses usually bring recession talk and rate-cut hopes.

connections.text: Both come from the same monthly jobs report.
The Fed reads this number closely.

usdcny.oneLine: How many Chinese yuan one US dollar buys.
usdcny.ifRising: Chinese goods usually get cheaper abroad, and trade politics usually sharpen.
usdcny.ifFalling: A softer dollar-yuan mix usually calms trade politics.

connections.text: A weaker yuan often appears when Chinese factories slow.

usdcny.australiaAngle: A weaker yuan often drags on the Australian dollar through the China trade channel.

michigan-1y-expectations.oneLine: What American households expect prices to do this coming year.
michigan-1y-expectations.ifRising: Households brace for higher inflation, which can feed wage demands.
michigan-1y-expectations.ifFalling: Americans usually feel calmer about prices ahead.

connections.text: This number rides inside the mood survey.
Worry tends to track what prices already did.

cfnai.oneLine: One score blending many US economic readings.
cfnai.ifRising: The US economy is usually running above its normal pace.
cfnai.ifFalling: Below-normal readings have historically clustered around downturns.

connections.text: Both measure the same economy; this one updates monthly.
Low stretches here usually line up with the recession model.

oecd-cli-cn.oneLine: A gauge that usually turns before China’s whole economy does.
oecd-cli-cn.ifRising: China’s direction is usually improving several months out.
oecd-cli-cn.ifFalling: A Chinese slowdown usually sits several months ahead.

connections.text: The monthly factory pulse confirms what this leads.
The US and China gauges frame world industry together.

oecd-cli-de.oneLine: A gauge that usually turns before Germany’s whole economy does.
oecd-cli-de.ifRising: Europe’s largest economy is usually improving several months out.
oecd-cli-de.ifFalling: A European slowdown usually sits several months ahead.

connections.text: Siblings in the same leading-indicator family.
German borrowing costs often echo the growth picture this leads.

epu-us.oneLine: How uncertain US policy news is right now.
epu-us.ifRising: Businesses usually delay investment and hiring decisions.
epu-us.ifFalling: A quieter policy backdrop usually lets plans proceed.

connections.text: The mood pair: policy noise beside household mood.

gpr-threats.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news is threats and warnings.
gpr-threats.ifRising: Markets usually price more caution when threats dominate coverage.
gpr-threats.ifFalling: A smaller threats share usually reads as a calmer news mix.

connections.text: The headline gauge this threat share belongs to.
The threats and acts pair splits the same coverage.

gpr-acts.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news is realised acts.
gpr-acts.ifRising: Coverage is shifting from warnings to actual events.
gpr-acts.ifFalling: Fewer acts in the news mix usually reads as de-escalation.

connections.text: The headline gauge this acts share belongs to.
The threats and acts pair splits the same coverage.

gpr-daily.oneLine: The war-and-tension news gauge, refreshed weekly.
gpr-daily.ifRising: A fresher read on the tension the monthly card reports.
gpr-daily.ifFalling: A fresher read on the calm the monthly card reports.

connections.text: The monthly average this weekly reading tracks.
The fear gauge often moves with tension news.

gpr-taiwan.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news mentions Taiwan.
gpr-taiwan.ifRising: A larger share of tension coverage is about Taiwan.
gpr-taiwan.ifFalling: A smaller share of tension coverage is about Taiwan.

connections.text: The headline gauge this country share belongs to.
The two east-Asia lenses of the same news stream.

gpr-china.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news mentions China.
gpr-china.ifRising: A larger share of tension coverage is about China.
gpr-china.ifFalling: A smaller share of tension coverage is about China.

connections.text: The headline gauge this country share belongs to.
Tension news beside China’s factory gauge.

gpr-russia.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news mentions Russia.
gpr-russia.ifRising: A larger share of tension coverage is about Russia.
gpr-russia.ifFalling: A smaller share of tension coverage is about Russia.

connections.text: The headline gauge this country share belongs to.
The pair usually moves together in this news stream.

gpr-ukraine.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news mentions Ukraine.
gpr-ukraine.ifRising: A larger share of tension coverage is about Ukraine.
gpr-ukraine.ifFalling: A smaller share of tension coverage is about Ukraine.

connections.text: The headline gauge this country share belongs to.
The pair usually moves together in this news stream.

gpr-israel.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news mentions Israel.
gpr-israel.ifRising: A larger share of tension coverage is about Israel.
gpr-israel.ifFalling: A smaller share of tension coverage is about Israel.

connections.text: The headline gauge this country share belongs to.
Middle-East tension often travels with the oil price.

gpr-saudi.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news mentions Saudi Arabia.
gpr-saudi.ifRising: A larger share of tension coverage is about Saudi Arabia.
gpr-saudi.ifFalling: A smaller share of tension coverage is about Saudi Arabia.

connections.text: The headline gauge this country share belongs to.
Gulf tension often travels with the oil price.

gpr-australia.oneLine: How much war-and-tension news mentions Australia.
gpr-australia.ifRising: A larger share of tension coverage is about Australia.
gpr-australia.ifFalling: A smaller share of tension coverage is about Australia.

connections.text: The headline gauge this country share belongs to.
Australia’s currency often reads the world mood.

tpu-us.oneLine: How much US policy news is about trade fights.
tpu-us.ifRising: Importers and exporters usually face harder planning.
tpu-us.ifFalling: A quieter trade-policy backdrop usually eases supply plans.

connections.text: The trade column of the wider policy-noise gauge.
Two lenses on world friction: trade words beside war words.

chokepoint-suez.oneLine: How many ships a day pass through the Suez Canal.
chokepoint-suez.ifRising: More of the Europe-Asia sea route is flowing through the canal.
chokepoint-suez.ifFalling: Fewer ships a day are using the Europe-Asia shortcut.

connections.text: The Red Sea gate on the canal’s southern approach.
The oil price often reads long freight routes into its moves.

chokepoint-panama.oneLine: How many ships a day pass through the Panama Canal.
chokepoint-panama.ifRising: More Atlantic-Pacific trade is moving through the canal.
chokepoint-panama.ifFalling: Fewer ships a day are crossing between the two oceans.

connections.text: The two canal gates between the world’s biggest trade blocs.
Longer freight routes tend to show up in oil’s price moves.

chokepoint-bab-el-mandeb.oneLine: How many ships a day pass the gate into the Red Sea.
chokepoint-bab-el-mandeb.ifRising: More Suez-bound traffic is taking the Red Sea route.
chokepoint-bab-el-mandeb.ifFalling: Fewer ships a day are entering the Red Sea gate.

connections.text: The canal the Red Sea gate feeds; the pair reads as one route.
The tension gauge of the region this gate sits in.

chokepoint-malacca.oneLine: How many ships a day pass between the Indian Ocean and east Asia.
chokepoint-malacca.ifRising: More of the Asia-bound trade is moving on the shortest sea lane.
chokepoint-malacca.ifFalling: Fewer ships a day are using the main east-Asia artery.

connections.text: The two busiest gates on the east-Asia approach.
Chinese factory runs tend to move with the raw-materials traffic.

chokepoint-taiwan.oneLine: How many ships a day pass through the Taiwan Strait.
chokepoint-taiwan.ifRising: More north-east Asian trade is moving through the strait.
chokepoint-taiwan.ifFalling: Fewer ships a day are crossing between mainland China and Taiwan.

connections.text: The two busiest gates on the east-Asia approach.
The tension gauge of the same waters, read beside the traffic.

copper-usd.oneLine: The world price of the metal that wires homes and grids.
copper-usd.ifRising: Wiring, appliances and building costs tend to climb.
copper-usd.ifFalling: A friend to builders, manufacturers and renovation budgets.

connections.text: Copper often moves with Chinese factory strength.
Copper is the growth leg of that metal measure.

stress-stlfsi.oneLine: One weekly number for stress across US money and credit markets.
stress-stlfsi.ifRising: Lending conditions usually tighten, in the US and often worldwide.
stress-stlfsi.ifFalling: Market plumbing usually calms, which often eases lending.

connections.text: The Chicago cousin reads the same stress with a wider lens.
Market fear usually rises with money-market stress.

nfci.oneLine: How easily money moves through the US financial system.
nfci.ifRising: Money usually gets harder to move, which slows lending.
nfci.ifFalling: Easy money usually supports credit and spending.

connections.text: The sister gauge from the St Louis Fed reads the same stress differently.

vix.oneLine: How nervous US share investors are right now.
vix.ifRising: Big, fast swings in world share markets usually loom.
vix.ifFalling: Calm usually settles over world share markets.

connections.text: War and tension news often lifts this gauge.
Fear and money-market stress usually move together.

gold-silver.oneLine: How many silver ounces one gold ounce buys.
gold-silver.ifRising: Fear usually leads, with gold the preferred safe haven.
gold-silver.ifFalling: Industrial strength usually shows, with silver running dearer.

connections.text: Gold is the fear leg of this measure.
Silver is the half-industrial leg.

cftc-gold-positioning.oneLine: How crowded big traders’ gold bets have become.
cftc-gold-positioning.ifRising: The gold trade usually gets crowded, the zone that unwinds hardest.
cftc-gold-positioning.ifFalling: Crowding usually thins; rare net-short stretches have sat near price floors.

connections.text: Stress plus crowding is the mix that unwinds hardest.
The bets being gauged are on this metal.

walcl.oneLine: The total size of what the US central bank owns.
walcl.ifRising: The system usually gets flooded with money, an emergency-style setting.
walcl.ifFalling: The Fed usually drains money steadily from the system.

connections.text: One is the central bank’s own creation of money; the other the banking system’s.
The Fed’s two levers: the price of money and the quantity.

crypto-fng.oneLine: A daily gauge of how fearful or greedy crypto markets feel.
crypto-fng.ifRising: Greed usually builds, and extreme greed has often appeared near sharp turns.
crypto-fng.ifFalling: Fear usually deepens; extreme fear has often sat near rebounds.

connections.text: The mood gauge and the Bitcoin price read the same market.

shiller-cape.oneLine: How expensive US shares look against their own long-run earnings power.
shiller-cape.ifRising: Shares get dearer against their earnings, which has often meant weaker decade-ahead returns.
shiller-cape.ifFalling: Cheaper shares, a mix that has often come with better decade-ahead returns.

connections.text: The companion reading puts shares against safe government money instead.
The safe-money leg of the companion reading is this real return.

shiller-ecy.oneLine: What US shares earn versus what safe US government money pays.
shiller-ecy.ifRising: Shares usually offer a fatter cushion over safe money.
shiller-ecy.ifFalling: Safe money usually competes harder, a mix that has weighed on decade-ahead returns.

connections.text: Both read the same share prices; this one subtracts safe money.

gpr-index.oneLine: How much war and tension fills the world’s news.
gpr-index.ifRising: Oil and gold usually climb, and shares often slip.
gpr-index.ifFalling: A calmer news backdrop usually supports risk-taking.

connections.text: The fear gauge often rises with war news.
Oil often jumps on war and supply scares.
Gold often rises on worry.

brent.oneLine: The world’s main oil price: what a barrel of crude costs.
brent.ifRising: Petrol, heating and delivery prices usually climb, feeding inflation nearly everywhere.
brent.ifFalling: Cheaper fuel usually eases household budgets and takes pressure off inflation.

connections.text: The American oil twin tracks this world price closely.
The storage-tanks card explains what oil prices are reacting to.
Costlier oil usually feeds into US inflation readings with a lag.

brent.australiaAngle: Australia imports much of its fuel, so local petrol prices usually track this oil price with a delay.

gold-usd.oneLine: The world price of one ounce of gold, in US dollars.
gold-usd.ifRising: Jewellery and coins usually cost more, often because money is seeking a safe haven.
gold-usd.ifFalling: Coins and jewellery usually get cheaper, often while worry fades.

connections.text: A stronger US dollar often weighs on this price.
Higher real yields tend to pull money away from gold.
Silver usually follows gold, only with bigger swings.

gold-usd.australiaAngle: Australians pay this price through the local dollar: a weaker AUD makes each ounce dearer locally.

silver-usd.oneLine: The world price of one ounce of silver, in US dollars.
silver-usd.ifRising: Jewellery and electronics usually cost more, and silver often swings harder than gold.
silver-usd.ifFalling: Metal costs usually ease for makers of electronics, solar panels and jewellery.

connections.text: Silver usually follows its bigger sibling, only harder.
This is one leg of the gold-versus-silver reading.

btc-usd.oneLine: The world price of one bitcoin, in US dollars.
btc-usd.ifRising: Crypto mood usually brightens across the whole family of digital assets.
btc-usd.ifFalling: Crypto mood usually darkens, and this famously jumpy asset can fall fast.

connections.text: The daily mood gauge reads the same market.
This price is the new-money leg of the bitcoin-versus-gold reading.

gold-btc.oneLine: How much gold one bitcoin buys.
gold-btc.ifRising: The market usually values the new digital money over the old metal money.
gold-btc.ifFalling: Gold usually holds its worth while bitcoin falls out of favour.

connections.text: Bitcoin is the new-money leg of this reading.
Gold is the old-money leg.

us-cpi-yoy.oneLine: How fast US consumer prices are rising, versus a year ago.
us-cpi-yoy.ifRising: Higher US inflation usually keeps world interest rates high for longer.
us-cpi-yoy.ifFalling: Cooling US inflation usually opens the door to cheaper borrowing worldwide.

connections.text: The Fed reacts to this number when moving its main rate.
The core companion strips the food and energy swings.
What households expect next year tends to follow this.

us-pce-core-yoy.oneLine: US inflation without food and energy, measured the Fed’s way.
us-pce-core-yoy.ifRising: The Fed usually stays tougher for longer, keeping world borrowing dearer.
us-pce-core-yoy.ifFalling: Cooling toward the Fed’s goal usually brings talk of cheaper money closer.

connections.text: The Fed’s stated inflation goal is defined on this measure.
Both read US prices; this one is the Fed’s own yardstick.
The other US core gauge reads the same stripped-out prices.

euro-hicp.oneLine: How fast prices are rising across the euro area.
euro-hicp.ifRising: The ECB usually keeps rates higher and euro loans dearer.
euro-hicp.ifFalling: Calmer euro-area inflation usually lets cheaper money return.

connections.text: The ECB’s policy rate answers this number.
The US and euro readings together frame world inflation.

breakeven-5y5y.oneLine: The US inflation rate markets expect five to ten years out.
breakeven-5y5y.ifRising: Markets are pricing more future inflation, the mood that keeps long rates high.
breakeven-5y5y.ifFalling: Markets fear weak future inflation, the setting that invites easy money.

connections.text: The ten-year companion reads the nearer window.
Expected inflation is one building block of long-term rates.
Central banks watch it to judge their credibility.

us-cpi-core-yoy.oneLine: US inflation with the jumpy food and energy prices taken out.
us-cpi-core-yoy.ifRising: A rising core usually keeps the Fed tough for longer.
us-cpi-core-yoy.ifFalling: A cooling core usually signals inflation fading at its roots.

connections.text: Both come from the same monthly price report.
The Fed’s core gauge reads the same underlying direction.

us-wages.oneLine: How fast American paychecks are growing, versus a year ago.
us-wages.ifRising: Faster pay sustains spending, but can feed inflation, the loop central banks watch.
us-wages.ifFalling: Pay growing slower than prices usually squeezes household budgets.

connections.text: The gap between this and price growth decides whether households gain ground.
The Fed watches the pay-and-price loop when setting rates.

breakeven-10y.oneLine: The US inflation rate markets expect over the next ten years.
breakeven-10y.ifRising: Bond markets are pricing more future inflation, which usually lifts long-term rates.
breakeven-10y.ifFalling: Markets fear weak inflation ahead, the setting that invites easy money.

connections.text: The far-ahead companion reads the window beyond five years.
The five-year companion reads the nearer window.
Expected inflation is one building block of the ten-year rate.

breakeven-tilt.plainName: The inflation tilt, near vs far
breakeven-tilt.oneLine: Whether markets price inflation building or fading into the far five years.
breakeven-tilt.ifRising: Markets lean toward inflation building into the far window, a mood that tends to lift long-run hedging.
breakeven-tilt.ifFalling: Markets lean toward inflation fading after the near window, reading today’s pressure as temporary.

connections.text: The near leg of the tilt: what markets price for the first five years.
The far leg of the tilt: the window beyond it.
The ten-year read blends both windows the tilt separates.

t5yie.oneLine: The US inflation rate markets expect over the next five years.
t5yie.ifRising: Markets are pricing more inflation over the medium term, usually lifting long rates.
t5yie.ifFalling: Markets fear soft inflation ahead, the setting that invites easy money.

connections.text: The ten-year companion reads the wider window.
The far-ahead companion reads beyond it.

wti.oneLine: What America pays for a barrel of its own crude.
wti.ifRising: US petrol and delivery prices usually climb, feeding into US inflation.
wti.ifFalling: Cheaper US oil usually eases American fuel costs and inflation pressure.

connections.text: The world twin usually trades close to this price.
The tanks gauge explains the supply side of this price.
Oil and gas together steer US household energy bills.

natgas.oneLine: The price of the gas that heats US homes and powers its grids.
natgas.ifRising: Winter heating and power bills in the US usually climb.
natgas.ifFalling: Cheaper gas usually eases heating and electricity bills for US households.

connections.text: Oil and gas together steer the energy line of household budgets.
Gas moves the energy line of US inflation readings.

eia-crude-stocks.oneLine: How much crude oil sits in America’s storage tanks.
eia-crude-stocks.ifRising: A glut usually builds, which has often dragged crude and pump prices down.
eia-crude-stocks.ifFalling: Draining tanks can signal a supply squeeze that pushes petrol prices up.

connections.text: Prices react to how full or empty the tanks run.
The American price reads these tanks closely.

platinum.oneLine: The world price of one ounce of platinum, in US dollars.
platinum.ifRising: Jewellery and the metal parts of cars usually cost more.
platinum.ifFalling: Cheaper platinum usually helps jewellers and car-part makers.

connections.text: The precious-metal cousin usually moves with gold, only harder.
Both metals straddle jewellery and factory demand.

gold-oil-ratio.oneLine: How many barrels of oil one ounce of gold buys.
gold-oil-ratio.ifRising: Gold usually buys more barrels, the mix that often marks fear-rich eras.
gold-oil-ratio.ifFalling: Each ounce usually buys fewer barrels, the mix that often marks energy-dominant eras.

connections.text: Gold is one leg of this reading.
Oil is the other leg.

food-index.oneLine: World food prices at the wholesale level, before they reach shelves.
food-index.ifRising: Grocery bills usually climb months later, hitting poorer households hardest.
food-index.ifFalling: Cheaper wholesale food usually brings relief to grocery budgets months ahead.

connections.text: Wheat is one ground-truth grain inside this basket.
Maize is the feed grain behind meat prices in the basket.
Food and fuel together move the household cost of living.

wheat.oneLine: What the world pays for a tonne of wheat.
wheat.ifRising: Flour, bread and animal-feed costs usually climb.
wheat.ifFalling: Cheaper wheat usually eases bread and feed budgets.

connections.text: The food basket leans on this staple grain.
The two grains swap in feed and food demand at times.

maize.oneLine: What the world pays for a tonne of maize.
maize.ifRising: Feed, meat and egg prices usually climb in its wake.
maize.ifFalling: Cheap feed usually eases meat and dairy budgets.

connections.text: The feed grain inside the food basket.
The two grains swap in feed and food demand at times.

au-cpi.oneLine: How fast Australian consumer prices are rising, versus a year ago.
au-cpi.ifRising: The RBA usually keeps rates higher, making loans dearer and saving pay more.
au-cpi.ifFalling: Cooling inflation usually opens the door to RBA rate cuts.

connections.text: The RBA moves its main rate in answer to this scoreboard.
The steadier companion shows the underlying direction.
Petrol is one of the jumpy items inside this basket.

au-cpi.australiaAngle: This is Australia’s own cost-of-living gauge: the number behind nearly every home-loan rate move.

au-trimmed-mean.oneLine: The steadier middle of Australian price changes that the RBA targets.
au-trimmed-mean.ifRising: A rising underlying reading usually keeps the RBA tough on rates.
au-trimmed-mean.ifFalling: Cooling underlying inflation usually opens the door to RBA cuts.

connections.text: The headline reading swings more; this one shows the steady core.
The RBA steers the cash rate by this reading first.

au-trimmed-mean.australiaAngle: The RBA’s preferred gauge: when it sits outside the target band, mortgage relief usually waits.

au-10y.oneLine: What the Australian government pays to borrow for ten years.
au-10y.ifRising: Fixed home-loan rates and term-deposit rates usually climb.
au-10y.ifFalling: Fixed home loans usually get cheaper and long savings pay less.

connections.text: The cash rate anchors the short end; this is the market’s long rate.
The gap card compares this yield with the US one.

au-10y.australiaAngle: This long rate, not just the cash rate, prices Australia’s multi-year money: fixed loans and term deposits follow it.

rba-expectations.plainName: Where markets think the RBA goes
rba-expectations.oneLine: Whether the market’s three-year rate sits above or below today’s cash rate.
rba-expectations.ifRising: Markets usually price a rising cash-rate path ahead.
rba-expectations.ifFalling: Markets usually price rate cuts ahead, the pattern that has opened past cutting cycles.

connections.text: The gap is measured against today’s cash rate.
The long-rate companion shows the ten-year window.

rba-expectations.australiaAngle: A positive gap usually means money is priced dearer ahead; a negative one has usually come before rate-cut cycles.

au-us-10y-gap.oneLine: Whether Australia pays more or less than the US to borrow for ten years.
au-us-10y-gap.ifRising: Global money usually finds Australian bonds more rewarding, supporting the local dollar.
au-us-10y-gap.ifFalling: US rates pulling above Australia’s have usually weighed on the local dollar.

connections.text: The Australian leg of the gap.
The US leg.
The dollar often follows this pull of money across the Pacific.

au-us-10y-gap.australiaAngle: This gap is one of the quiet levers on the Australian dollar: when the US pays clearly more, the AUD usually sags.

au-petrol-yoy.oneLine: How much more or less Australian fuel costs than a year ago.
au-petrol-yoy.ifRising: Family budgets and freight costs usually feel the squeeze first.
au-petrol-yoy.ifFalling: Cheaper fuel is the rare reading that eases household budgets.

connections.text: Fuel is a jumpy item inside the inflation basket.
World oil and the local dollar usually drive the pump together.

au-petrol-yoy.australiaAngle: The bowser is Australia’s most visible weekly price; it feeds headline inflation and the RBA’s mood.

rba-cash-rate.oneLine: Australia’s main interest rate, set by the Reserve Bank.
rba-cash-rate.ifRising: Variable home loans and savings rates usually follow within weeks.
rba-cash-rate.ifFalling: Borrowers usually get relief and savers earn less, with a lag.

connections.text: The Fed sets the US twin of this dial.
Home-loan rates follow this dial with a lag.
Savings rates ride on it too.

rba-cash-rate.australiaAngle: Every variable mortgage in Australia reprices with this dial; savings accounts follow.

au-unemployment.oneLine: The share of Australians looking for work who cannot find it.
au-unemployment.ifRising: Job hunting usually gets harder and household spending softer.
au-unemployment.ifFalling: Plentiful jobs usually support wages and confidence.

connections.text: Vacancies usually turn before the jobless rate does.
The RBA watches the jobs market when setting rates.

au-unemployment.australiaAngle: A half-point rise off a low has often marked the start of an Australian slowdown.

au-wage-growth.oneLine: How fast Australian wages are rising, versus a year ago.
au-wage-growth.ifRising: Pay packets usually catch up, though fast pay can feed prices.
au-wage-growth.ifFalling: An hour’s pay usually covers less when prices keep rising.

connections.text: The gap between this and price growth shows whether pay is winning.
A strong jobs market usually keeps pay rising.

au-wage-growth.australiaAngle: The wage-and-price scoreboard: through much of Australia’s inflation era, pay lagged prices, squeezing real budgets.

au-rent-yoy.oneLine: How fast Australian rents are rising, versus a year ago.
au-rent-yoy.ifRising: Renters’ budgets usually squeeze harder at renewal time.
au-rent-yoy.ifFalling: Weak rent growth is the rare relief for renters’ budgets.

connections.text: Rent is a big weight inside the inflation basket.
Rent and house prices often move together, but not always.
Rate moves usually cool the housing market with a delay.

au-rent-yoy.australiaAngle: Rent is the biggest weekly bill for roughly a third of Australian households.

au-home-loan.oneLine: The average rate on outstanding Australian home loans.
au-home-loan.ifRising: Monthly repayments usually rise, squeezing household budgets.
au-home-loan.ifFalling: Relief usually reaches variable loans first, with a lag.

connections.text: Each cash-rate move flows into this rate with a lag.
The savings twin: what the crowd pays versus earns.
The US twin shows the American home-loan story.

au-home-loan.australiaAngle: Home loans are the biggest debt of most Australian households; this is the rate they actually pay.

au-deposit-rate.oneLine: What banks pay on new household term deposits.
au-deposit-rate.ifRising: Savers shopping today usually find more interest on offer.
au-deposit-rate.ifFalling: Cash savings usually earn less, and locking money away pays less too.

connections.text: Term-deposit rates usually track the cash rate with a short lag.
The borrowing twin of this savings rate.
Real saving power depends on the gap to inflation.

au-deposit-rate.australiaAngle: The twin of the mortgage card: what the crowd earns on savings while borrowers pay the loan rate.

au-home-values.oneLine: The average price of Australian homes, as an index.
au-home-values.ifRising: Owners feel richer and first-home buyers usually face a harder climb.
au-home-values.ifFalling: Cheaper homes usually make entering easier, but rarely last long in Australia.

connections.text: New lending usually turns before home values do.
Rate rises have usually cooled the market, with a delay.

au-home-values.australiaAngle: Housing is the biggest asset and debt source for Australian households; prices feed wealth and confidence.

au-household-debt-arrears.oneLine: How large Australian household debt sits against income.
au-household-debt-arrears.ifRising: Every rate rise usually bites harder, and arrears tend to follow with a lag.
au-household-debt-arrears.ifFalling: Household balance sheets usually mend, softening the blow of rate moves.

connections.text: High debt is why RBA moves dominate Australian household budgets.
Home loans are the biggest slice of this debt.

au-household-debt-arrears.australiaAngle: Australian households carry among the world’s heaviest debt loads, so rate moves dominate the national mood.

au-housing-finance.oneLine: How much Australians are borrowing for homes right now.
au-housing-finance.ifRising: Households are committing; housing demand usually builds ahead.
au-housing-finance.ifFalling: Households stepping back is usually the leading edge of a housing slowdown.

connections.text: Loans are signed months before they show up in home values.
Lending usually cools after rate rises and warms after cuts.

au-housing-finance.australiaAngle: The Australian leading edge: a loan commitment turns first, home values follow.

au-job-vacancies.oneLine: How many jobs Australian employers are trying to fill.
au-job-vacancies.ifRising: Employers are usually still hungry to hire; a strong jobs market.
au-job-vacancies.ifFalling: Employers usually pull back here before unemployment rises.

connections.text: One leads, one lags: vacancies first, joblessness second.
Hiring strength is one input the RBA reads.

au-job-vacancies.australiaAngle: Vacancies usually roll over long before joblessness does, the early-warning line for Australia.

au-saving-ratio.oneLine: The share of income Australian households save.
au-saving-ratio.ifRising: Caution is usually rising, and spending often softens before income does.
au-saving-ratio.ifFalling: Households are usually either stretched or confident enough to spend it all.

connections.text: Caution and borrowing usually move in opposite directions.
A saving cushion softens the sting of price rises.

au-saving-ratio.australiaAngle: The hunkering-down gauge: when uncertainty rises, Australian households save more and spend less first.

audusd.oneLine: How many US dollars one Australian dollar buys.
audusd.ifRising: Imports and overseas travel usually get cheaper for Australians.
audusd.ifFalling: Imports and travel usually get dearer, while exports earn more abroad.

connections.text: The rate gap between the two central banks pulls this pair.
Commodity booms usually lift the Australian dollar.
This pair is one thread in the dollar’s overall strength.

audusd.australiaAngle: Australia’s key pair: it prices imports, exports and overseas travel in one number.

audjpy.oneLine: How many Japanese yen one Australian dollar buys.
audjpy.ifRising: Travel to Japan usually gets cheaper for Australians, and risk appetite usually builds.
audjpy.ifFalling: A fast fall is the classic world de-risking signal, as borrowed yen rushes home.

connections.text: The US-Japan rate gap keeps the carry trade alive behind this pair.
The dollar’s own strength often shows up here too.
The Bank of Japan anchors the yen side.

audjpy.australiaAngle: A watched world risk barometer, and the rate that matters for Australian travel and shopping in Japan.

terms-of-trade.oneLine: Whether Australia’s export prices beat its import prices.
terms-of-trade.ifRising: The country usually gets richer without shipping anything more.
terms-of-trade.ifFalling: National income usually squeezes, along with budgets and the dollar.

connections.text: Iron ore is the biggest export weight in this measure.
Export-versus-import strength usually steers the dollar over the years.

terms-of-trade.australiaAngle: Mining booms send it soaring and lift Australian budgets, jobs and the dollar together.

rba-fed-gap.oneLine: How far Australia’s main rate sits above or below America’s.
rba-fed-gap.ifRising: The carry trade usually earns more here, drawing money toward the Australian dollar.
rba-fed-gap.ifFalling: Money usually leaves for the higher US yield, weighing on the Australian dollar.

connections.text: This gap is a key pull on the key pair.
The RBA side of the gap.
The Fed side.

rba-fed-gap.australiaAngle: The short-term money pull between the two dollars: a wide gap either way usually moves the AUD.

gold-aud.oneLine: The world gold price, converted into Australian dollars.
gold-aud.ifRising: Coins, jewellery and local metal usually cost more in Australia.
gold-aud.ifFalling: Local buyers usually get the rare discount on the metal.

connections.text: The world price is the main ingredient of the local one.
A weaker local dollar usually makes gold dearer in Australia.

gold-aud.australiaAngle: For coins, jewellery and metal funds priced in Australia, this is the real price, not the US-dollar one.

iron-ore.oneLine: The world price of iron ore, Australia’s single biggest export.
iron-ore.ifRising: Mining jobs, company profits and government budgets usually fatten.
iron-ore.ifFalling: Pressure usually builds on mining profits, budgets and the dollar.

connections.text: Iron ore is the biggest weight in Australia’s export prices.
Chinese factory strength usually drives this demand.
The dollar often rides on iron-ore fortunes.

iron-ore.australiaAngle: Iron ore funds Australian miners, budgets and the broader export-price story, and China’s building cycle dominates its demand.

n225.oneLine: One number for how Japan’s largest companies are doing.
n225.ifRising: Big Japanese firms are faring well, often a sign of healthy world trade.
n225.ifFalling: Japan’s big firms are struggling; a strong yen or weak world demand is often behind it.

connections.text: Japan’s market usually moves with the yen; a cheaper yen helps its exporters.
The yen-jump alarm reads this market beside the dollar-yen pair.

asx200.oneLine: One number for how Australia’s largest listed companies are doing.
asx200.ifRising: Australian companies are doing well, often with firm iron-ore and metal prices.
asx200.ifFalling: Australian companies are under pressure, usually from weaker iron-ore prices or soft Chinese demand.

connections.text: The home market follows iron ore closely.
Chinese factory strength usually steers Australian company fortunes.
A firm home market and a firm local dollar sometimes move together.

kospi.oneLine: One number for how South Korea’s largest companies are doing.
kospi.ifRising: Korean chipmakers and exporters are doing well, often a sign of strong world electronics demand.
kospi.ifFalling: Korea’s exporters are struggling, usually on weaker demand for phones, cars and chips.

connections.text: Korea’s market usually follows America’s lead.
The two Asian hubs often share the same regional mood.

hsi.oneLine: One number for how Hong Kong’s largest companies are doing.
hsi.ifRising: Investors often feel better about Chinese business, and money is flowing into Hong Kong.
hsi.ifFalling: Investors are often worried about China’s economy or politics, and money is leaving Hong Kong.

connections.text: Both read China’s mood from different doors.
China’s factory strength often lifts both doors.

ssec.oneLine: One number for how companies listed in Shanghai are doing.
ssec.ifRising: China’s home economy and its shoppers often look stronger, lifting demand for oil and metals.
ssec.ifFalling: China’s home market is struggling; its demand for oil, metals and many imports often cools too.

connections.text: Factory strength usually leads the home market’s mood.
China buys much of Australia’s iron ore, so this mood reaches Australian exports.

taiex.oneLine: One number for how Taiwan’s largest companies are doing.
taiex.ifRising: The world’s appetite for advanced chips is usually strong, a healthy sign for technology everywhere.
taiex.ifFalling: Chip demand is often cooling, or investors are pricing trouble around Taiwan.

connections.text: Both ride the world’s chip cycle.
America’s technology mood usually washes over Taiwan’s.

nifty50.oneLine: One number for how India’s largest companies are doing.
nifty50.ifRising: Investors usually feel confident about India’s fast-growing economy and are putting money in.
nifty50.ifFalling: Foreign money is often leaving India, usually on worries about its growth or world risk appetite.

connections.text: India and China sometimes compete for the same global investor money.
Falls in America often pull money out of emerging markets like India.

stoxx50.oneLine: One number for how the euro area’s largest companies are doing.
stoxx50.ifRising: European business is doing well, often a sign of healthy world trade and steady European demand.
stoxx50.ifFalling: European business is struggling, often with worry about the euro area’s economy.

connections.text: The German and euro-wide lists usually tell one European story.
Europe’s health often shows in its money too.
The Europe-worry alarm reads this list beside the euro-franc pair.

dax.oneLine: One number for how Germany’s largest companies are doing.
dax.ifRising: German factories and exporters are usually busy, a good sign for world trade.
dax.ifFalling: German industry is struggling, often an early sign of slowing world trade.

connections.text: The German leading indicator usually turns with this market.
Germany is the euro area’s biggest economy; its list usually leads Europe’s.
China’s demand pulls hard on German exports.

cac.oneLine: One number for how France’s largest companies are doing.
cac.ifRising: French business is doing well, often with luxury brands, banks and energy firms in demand.
cac.ifFalling: French business is under pressure, often with soft spending at home or weaker world demand.

connections.text: France and Germany usually tell one European story.
France’s list is a big slice of Europe’s widest one.
France’s list usually moves with the euro too.

ftse.oneLine: One number for how the biggest London-listed companies are doing.
ftse.ifRising: The global mining, oil and banking giants usually earn well, since most make their money abroad.
ftse.ifFalling: The world-facing giants usually struggle, often with oil and metal prices down too.

connections.text: A big slice of this list sells oil, so Brent often moves it.
The pound usually tells a UK story beside this world-facing list.

sp500.oneLine: One number for how the largest US companies are doing.
sp500.ifRising: US business is confident, and world markets usually follow America’s lead higher.
sp500.ifFalling: US companies are under pressure, and markets almost everywhere often follow it down.

connections.text: The market fear gauge usually climbs when this list falls.
The two most-quoted US lists usually tell one story; this one is the broader.
The money-hiding alarm reads this list beside the dollar and gold.

ndx.oneLine: One number for how big US technology and growth companies are doing.
ndx.ifRising: Investors usually want technology and growth stories, and are comfortable taking risk.
ndx.ifFalling: Investors are often pulling back from technology and pricier growth stories.

connections.text: This list usually swings harder than the broad one.
Falls here often ripple into crypto.
The chip chain links Taiwan’s list to this one.

dow.oneLine: The most-quoted number for US company shares.
dow.ifRising: America’s best-known companies are doing well, often lifting the mood of markets that open next.
dow.ifFalling: America’s best-known companies are falling, often souring the mood of markets that open after New York.

connections.text: Both tell the US story; the broad list is the better measure.
The technology list reads the same country, louder.

tsx.oneLine: One number for how Canada’s largest companies are doing.
tsx.ifRising: Canadian energy, banking and mining firms usually earn well, often with firm oil and metal prices.
tsx.ifFalling: Canadian firms usually struggle, often with oil and metal prices down too.

connections.text: Canada sells a lot of oil, so Brent often moves this list.
Canada’s market usually follows its giant next-door neighbour.

ibov.oneLine: One number for how Brazil’s largest companies are doing.
ibov.ifRising: Investors usually feel fine about riskier emerging markets and raw-material exporters.
ibov.ifFalling: Investors are often fleeing riskier markets, usually with a stronger US dollar nearby.

connections.text: Emerging-market falls usually go with broad dollar strength.
Brazil’s oil and mining giants ride world raw-material prices.

eurusd.oneLine: How many US dollars one euro buys.
eurusd.ifRising: A stronger euro usually makes dollar-priced goods cheaper for people earning euros.
eurusd.ifFalling: A weaker euro usually makes imports and travel dearer for people earning euros.

connections.text: The euro is the biggest single weight in the dollar basket.
The European Central Bank steers the euro’s side.
The dollar-or-euro pattern explains this pair’s moves.

gbpusd.oneLine: How many US dollars one British pound buys.
gbpusd.ifRising: A stronger pound usually makes dollar-priced goods and travel cheaper for Britons.
gbpusd.ifFalling: A weaker pound usually makes imports and US travel dearer for Britons.

connections.text: The Bank of England steers the pound’s side.
The pound is one thread in the dollar’s overall strength.

usdchf.oneLine: How many Swiss francs one US dollar buys.
usdchf.ifRising: The dollar usually gains on the franc through broad strength or as world worry fades.
usdchf.ifFalling: The franc usually gains on the dollar, often a sign of worry somewhere in the world.

connections.text: The franc is one thread in the dollar’s overall strength.
Europe’s worry pair reads this same franc.

eurjpy.oneLine: How many Japanese yen one euro buys.
eurjpy.ifRising: A stronger euro against the yen often goes with calm world moods and cheaper Japan trips for Europeans.
eurjpy.ifFalling: A falling euro against the yen usually means worried investors are rushing back into the yen.

connections.text: The Australian-dollar pair reads the same mood; a shared fall is the stronger signal.
The euro’s own health shows in both pairs.
The Bank of Japan anchors the yen side.

eurchf.oneLine: How many Swiss francs one euro buys.
eurchf.ifRising: The euro gaining on the franc often means worry about Europe is fading.
eurchf.ifFalling: The franc usually gains when investors worry about Europe; a fast fall is a classic warning.

connections.text: The Europe-worry alarm reads this pair beside Europe’s main company list.
This pattern card is built around this pair.

audcny.oneLine: How many Chinese yuan one Australian dollar buys.
audcny.ifRising: The Australian dollar usually gains on the yuan when China’s demand looks healthy.
audcny.ifFalling: The Australian dollar usually sags against the yuan when China’s economy cools.

connections.text: Iron ore is the biggest trade behind the link.
The yuan against the US dollar is this pair’s other half.
The China-link pattern watches exactly these two legs.

r1_risk_mood.oneLine: When money is calm, the Australian dollar and US stocks usually move together.
r1_risk_mood.skipReason: This card tracks a link between two moving lines, not a level that rises or falls on its own.

connections.text: The mood leg: a growth currency priced in yen.
The mood’s other leg: America’s main company list.
A second yen pair often confirms the same mood.

r2_carry_trade.oneLine: A sudden yen surge usually shakes the carry trade and world markets.
r2_carry_trade.skipReason: This card tracks a link between two moving lines, not a level that rises or falls on its own.

connections.text: The pair this alarm reads.
The stock leg: Japan’s main company list.
The rate gap that keeps this trade alive.

r3_dollar_strength.oneLine: The US dollar and gold usually move in opposite directions.
r3_dollar_strength.skipReason: This card tracks a link between two moving lines, not a level that rises or falls on its own.

connections.text: The dollar leg: the dollar against six big currencies.
The gold leg: the world price of an ounce.
Higher US lending returns often lift the dollar and weigh on gold.

r4_money_hiding.oneLine: In a scare money usually runs to the US dollar; if it leaves, gold often shines.
r4_money_hiding.skipReason: This card tracks a link between three moving lines, not a level that rises or falls on its own.

connections.text: The risk leg: America’s main company list.
The safety leg: the dollar against six currencies.
The second safety leg: the world gold price.

r5_china_link.oneLine: China’s demand usually moves the Australian dollar and the yuan in mirror-image ways.
r5_china_link.skipReason: This card tracks a link between two moving lines, not a level that rises or falls on its own.

connections.text: One leg: Australia’s key pair.
The other leg: the yuan against the dollar.
The trade behind the link: iron ore, China’s biggest import from Australia.

r6_europe_worry.oneLine: When Europe worries, the euro usually slips against the franc and European companies fall.
r6_europe_worry.skipReason: This card tracks a link between two moving lines, not a level that rises or falls on its own.

connections.text: The money leg: the euro against Switzerland’s franc.
The company leg: Europe’s main company list.
The European Central Bank’s rate often steers Europe’s mood.

r7_dollar_or_euro.oneLine: Tells whether euro-versus-dollar moves are a dollar story or a euro story.
r7_dollar_or_euro.skipReason: This card separates two possible causes behind one move, not a level that rises or falls on its own.

connections.text: The pair being explained.
The yardstick that separates the two stories.
A weak-euro story often shows here too.

nyfed-custody.plainName: Foreign official holdings, New York Fed
nyfed-custody.oneLine: The US government debt that foreign central banks and governments keep at the New York Fed.
nyfed-custody.ifRising: Foreign central banks and governments are usually adding to their US Treasury holdings.
nyfed-custody.ifFalling: Foreign central banks and governments are usually reducing them.

term-premium-10y.oneLine: The extra yield investors demand for lending to the US for ten years.
term-premium-10y.ifRising: Investors are demanding more to commit money long-term.
term-premium-10y.ifFalling: Long-term lending is being priced closer to the path of short rates.

connections.text: The 10-year yield splits into the policy outlook plus this premium.
Both are ways the long end prices risk and inflation.

term-premium-10y.australiaAngle: A rising US term premium tends to lift long-term yields worldwide, and Australian long-term rates usually feel that pull.

tga.oneLine: The US government’s own bank balance at the Federal Reserve.
tga.ifRising: Bond sales and taxes are pulling cash into the government’s till.
tga.ifFalling: Government spending is pushing cash back into the system.

connections.text: The account is subtracted there: that cash is not in the system.
The Fed’s balance sheet funds it on the other side of the ledger.

reverse-repo.oneLine: Cash parked at the Federal Reserve overnight instead of reaching private markets.
reverse-repo.ifRising: More money is choosing the Fed’s floor over lending anywhere else.
reverse-repo.ifFalling: That cash is moving back into markets and bills.

connections.text: The pile is subtracted there: parked cash is not available cash.
The two sides of the system’s spare cash.

bank-reserves.oneLine: The deposits banks keep at the Federal Reserve: the system’s liquidity buffer.
bank-reserves.ifRising: The buffer behind the banking system is filling.
bank-reserves.ifFalling: The buffer is thinning, the setting where funding pressure tends to appear.

connections.text: Pressure there with falling reserves is the classic squeeze pattern.
Reserves are a liability the balance sheet creates.

repo-stress.oneLine: How much more overnight money costs than what the Fed pays banks: the plumbing’s stress gauge.
repo-stress.ifRising: Borrowers are paying up for overnight cash.
repo-stress.ifFalling: Cash is easy, trading at or below the Fed’s own rate.

connections.text: The card’s own upper leg.
A thinning reserve buffer is what usually drives the gap up.

net-liquidity.oneLine: The money actually available to markets after subtracting the Treasury account and reverse repos.
net-liquidity.ifRising: The pool supporting trading and lending is growing.

connections.text: The headline the net measure starts from.
One of the two drains subtracted.
The other drain subtracted.

net-liquidity.australiaAngle: When US net liquidity drains, dollar funding tightens globally, and Australian banks usually pay more for offshore US-dollar funding.

ebp.oneLine: How much extra investors demand to lend to risky companies, beyond covering the losses they expect.
ebp.ifRising: Lenders are charging more for risk appetite itself, not just for expected defaults.
ebp.ifFalling: Credit is priced closer to expected losses alone: the pure risk-appetite charge is coming down.

connections.text: A rising premium feeds the same strain the stress index folds together.
One is the extra charge for lending long to the government; this one for lending to companies.

ofr-fsi.oneLine: The Treasury’s own daily score of how strained money markets are (zero = its long-run average).
ofr-fsi.ifRising: Strains in credit, funding or volatility are building together.
ofr-fsi.ifFalling: The system is calmer than its long-run average.

connections.text: The St Louis twin: same question, different builder.
Funding pressure is one of the channels this index folds in.

gdpnow.oneLine: The Atlanta Fed’s running estimate of this quarter’s US growth.
gdpnow.ifRising: This quarter is tracking stronger as the data lands.
gdpnow.ifFalling: This quarter is tracking weaker as the data lands.

connections.text: The official print for the quarter before; this nowcast runs the current one.
Consumer spending is the biggest input the model aggregates.

empire-state.oneLine: A monthly survey of New York manufacturers: above zero means growth.
empire-state.ifRising: More New York manufacturers are reporting growth than decline.
empire-state.ifFalling: More New York manufacturers are reporting decline than growth.

connections.text: The same question asked of Philadelphia factories.
Factory surveys often turn before the headline growth number.

continuing-claims.oneLine: The number of people already receiving unemployment benefits each week.
continuing-claims.ifRising: Fewer people are ending up off the rolls: job-finding is slowing.
continuing-claims.ifFalling: People are leaving the rolls faster: job-finding is picking up.

connections.text: One counts new filings; this counts everyone still claiming.
The monthly rate the weekly rolls feed into.

median-cpi.oneLine: US inflation measured by the middle price change, ignoring the wildest moves.
median-cpi.ifRising: The steady middle of price changes is moving up.
median-cpi.ifFalling: The steady middle of price changes is coming down.

connections.text: The headline measure this middle read sits beside.
Both strip noise from the monthly print, each a different way.

sticky-cpi.oneLine: US inflation in the goods and services that rarely change price.
sticky-cpi.ifRising: Even rarely-changing prices are rising faster: underlying pressure is building.
sticky-cpi.ifFalling: Even rarely-changing prices are cooling: underlying pressure is coming down.

connections.text: The other quiet-inflation read, built the opposite way.
The headline print the sticky basket reads beside.

sloos-ci-tightening.oneLine: The net share of US banks making business loans harder to get.
sloos-ci-tightening.ifRising: More banks are making business loans harder to obtain.
sloos-ci-tightening.ifFalling: Fewer banks are making business loans hard to obtain.

connections.text: One is the price of lending to companies; this is the gate.
A rising share here has usually lined up with weaker growth.

us-deficit-12m.oneLine: How much the US government borrowed over the last twelve months.
us-deficit-12m.ifRising: The government is borrowing more, adding to the supply of bonds the market has to absorb.
us-deficit-12m.ifFalling: The government is borrowing less, and the flow of new bonds is coming down.

connections.text: One is the borrowing flow; that one the interest bill it grows.
More bonds to place is one of the pressures yields answer to.

us-deficit-monthly.oneLine: What the US government borrowed or repaid in the latest month alone.
us-deficit-monthly.ifRising: The month’s borrowing gap is widening.
us-deficit-monthly.ifFalling: The month’s borrowing gap is narrowing.

treasury-auction-10y.oneLine: How many dollars chased each dollar of 10-year bonds at the latest auction.
treasury-auction-10y.ifRising: Buyers bid more for each dollar of 10-year bonds: stronger demand.
treasury-auction-10y.ifFalling: Buyers bid less for each dollar of 10-year bonds: thinner demand.

connections.text: The same question for the long bond.
The supply the auctions answer for.

treasury-auction-10y-indirect.oneLine: The share of the latest 10-year auction taken by indirect bidders.
treasury-auction-10y-indirect.ifRising: Indirect bidders took a bigger share of the 10-year auction.
treasury-auction-10y-indirect.ifFalling: Indirect bidders took a smaller share of the 10-year auction.

treasury-auction-30y.oneLine: How many dollars chased each dollar of 30-year bonds at the latest auction.
treasury-auction-30y.ifRising: Buyers bid more for each dollar of long bonds: stronger demand.
treasury-auction-30y.ifFalling: Buyers bid less for each dollar of long bonds: thinner demand.

connections.text: The same question for the 10-year note.
The yield the auctions clear against.

treasury-auction-30y-indirect.oneLine: The share of the latest 30-year auction taken by indirect bidders.
treasury-auction-30y-indirect.ifRising: Indirect bidders took a bigger share of the 30-year auction.
treasury-auction-30y-indirect.ifFalling: Indirect bidders took a smaller share of the 30-year auction.

inflation.plain: How fast prices are rising. Higher inflation means the same money buys less over time.
inflation.example: If inflation is 3%, something that cost $100 last year costs about $103 now.

core-inflation.plain: Inflation with food and energy prices taken out. It shows the steadier direction underneath the noisy monthly moves.

trimmed-mean.plain: An inflation reading that drops the wildest price rises and falls each month before averaging. It shows the steady middle of price changes.

deflation.plain: When prices are falling on average. It sounds good but can stall an economy and wages.

interest-rate.plain: The price of borrowing money. Higher rates make loans cost more and make saving pay more.

policy-rate.plain: The central bank’s main interest rate. It steers savings, loan and bond rates across the economy.

bond.plain: A loan you give to a government or a company. They pay you interest and give the money back later.

yield.plain: The yearly return you get from lending money through a bond.

real-yield.plain: A bond yield after taking out expected inflation. It shows the real return a lender keeps.

yield-curve.plain: The shape of interest rates from short to long borrowing times. A flat or inverted curve is a classic warning.

breakeven.plain: The inflation rate markets are pricing, from the gap between a normal bond and an inflation-linked bond of the same length.

central-bank.plain: The institution that controls a country’s interest rates and money supply, like the Reserve Bank of Australia or the US Fed.

recession.plain: A period when a country’s economy shrinks and more people lose jobs.

volatility.plain: How wildly prices jump around. High volatility means big, fast swings.

safe-haven.plain: Something people tend to move money into when they are worried, like gold.

commodity.plain: A raw material bought and sold in bulk, like oil, gold or wheat.

stock-index.plain: One number that tracks how a group of big companies’ shares is doing overall.

mortgage.plain: A loan used to purchase a home, paid back with interest over many years.

carry-trade.plain: Borrowing money where it is cheap, like Japan, and putting it to work where it pays more. When the interest gap between the two sides shrinks, these trades usually unwind fast.

pmi.plain: A monthly survey of factory purchasing managers. Readings above the halfway line mean factories are getting busier; below means quieter.
pmi.example: The halfway mark is 50: a reading of 52 means factories are growing a little, 48 means shrinking a little.

vix.plain: A number the market prices from the size of the swings it sees coming in America’s main share index. It usually jumps when worry spreads.

money-supply.plain: The total amount of money sitting in bank accounts and circulating in an economy. It grows when banks lend a lot.

leading-indicator.plain: A measure that usually turns before the whole economy does. It is watched for early hints, never promises.

treasury-securities.plain: Loans to the US government: Treasury bills, notes and bonds. Foreign governments and investors hold trillions of dollars of them.

foreign-official-holdings.plain: The part held by foreign central banks and governments, as opposed to private investors abroad.

net-purchases.plain: What investors actually bought minus what they sold over a period. It measures real buying or selling, not price changes.

valuation-change.plain: The change in what existing holdings are worth as market prices move. When yields rise, bond values fall, so holdings can shrink with no selling at all.

custody-hub.plain: A country whose reported holdings include much that belongs to investors elsewhere, because the securities are simply held there. Belgium, Luxembourg, the Cayman Islands, Ireland, the UK, Switzerland and Bermuda are the big ones.

liquidity.plain: How easily money can be had in a market: cash ready to use, rather than tied up in assets.

term-premium.plain: The extra yield investors demand for lending long-term instead of rolling short-term loans, on top of the path of short rates.

treasury-general-account.plain: The US government’s own bank account at the Federal Reserve, from which it pays its bills.

reverse-repo.plain: An overnight deposit at the Federal Reserve: money funds and others park cash there at a set rate instead of lending it in private markets.

bank-reserves.plain: The deposits banks keep at the central bank. They are the raw material of the overnight lending market between banks.

net-liquidity.plain: The money actually available to markets: the Fed’s balance sheet minus the Treasury’s account and the overnight cash parked back at the Fed.

excess-bond-premium.plain: The part of what investors demand for lending to risky companies that is NOT compensation for expected losses — the pure extra charge for risk appetite itself.

financial-stress-index.plain: A daily score of how strained money markets are. The OFR’s own combines credit, funding, volatility, safe-asset and equity-valuation pressure into one number around zero (zero = its long-run average).

nowcast.plain: An estimate of something happening right now, built from data that arrives before the official number. “Now” plus “forecast”: no waiting, less certainty.
nowcast.example: The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow estimates this quarter’s growth while the quarter is still running.

bid-to-cover.plain: How many dollars were bid for every dollar of bonds a Treasury auction sold. A lower reading says demand was thinner.
bid-to-cover.example: A bid-to-cover of 2.5 means buyers offered two and a half dollars for every dollar of bonds sold — around 2.5 has been typical.

chokepoint.plain: A narrow sea passage that a large share of world shipping passes through, such as a canal or a strait between two land masses.
chokepoint.example: The Suez Canal, the Panama Canal and the Strait of Malacca are the best-known chokepoints.

transit-estimate.plain: One ship passing through a passage, counted once. The count is an estimate from ship-tracking data, so it can be revised.

ui.noDirection: Direction does not give a clear signal here

yield-curve-10y2y.oneLine: فاصلهٔ وام بلندمدت و کوتاه‌مدت دولت آمریکا.
yield-curve-10y2y.ifRising: باز کردن این فاصله معمولاً با رشد یا فشار تورم همراه است.
yield-curve-10y2y.ifFalling: فاصلهٔ کوچک یا منفی پیش از بیشتر رکودهای آمریکا رخ داده است.

connections.text: هر دو یک سیگنال رکود را از دو زاویه می‌خوانند.

yield-curve-10y3m.oneLine: فاصله‌ای که خود فدرال رزرو بیش از همه زیر نظر دارد.
yield-curve-10y3m.ifRising: فاصلهٔ شیب‌دار معمولاً با رشد یا فشار تورم همراه است.
yield-curve-10y3m.ifFalling: معکوس‌های عمیق این بازو پیش از هر رکود مدرن آمریکا رخ داده است.

connections.text: بازوی ۳ ماهه و مدل رکود یک داستان می‌گویند.

real-yield-10y.plainName: بازده وام آمریکا پس از تورم
real-yield-10y.oneLine: سودی که وام دادن به دولت آمریکا پس از کسر تورم دارد.
real-yield-10y.ifRising: پس‌انداز امن بیشتر می‌سازد، پس دارایی‌های بدون سود مثل طلا اغلب جذابیت کمتری پیدا می‌کنند.
real-yield-10y.ifFalling: نگه‌داشتن پول امن پس از تورم کم سود می‌دهد، که اغلب به دارایی‌های بدون سود کمک می‌کند.

connections.text: بازده واقعی بالاتر معمولاً بر طلا فشار می‌آورد.

real-yield-10y.australiaAngle: بازده واقعی بالای آمریکا معمولاً بر دلار استرالیا و قیمت طلا فشار می‌آورد.

us10y.oneLine: نرخ بهرهٔ بدهی ۱۰ سالهٔ دولت آمریکا.
us10y.ifRising: وام مسکن و اعتبار کسب‌وکار معمولاً با فاصله‌ای پیروی می‌کنند.
us10y.ifFalling: ارزان‌تر شدن وام معمولاً به وام‌ها و قیمت دارایی‌ها کمک می‌کند.

connections.text: وام مسکن ۳۰ سالهٔ آمریکا از اوراق ۱۰ سالهٔ آمریکا پیروی می‌کند.
بازده نامی تقریباً برابر است با بازده واقعی به‌علاوهٔ تورم مورد انتظار.

us10y.australiaAngle: نرخ‌های بلندمدت و دلار استرالیا معمولاً با نرخ‌های بلندمدت آمریکا حرکت می‌کنند.

us30y.oneLine: نرخ بهرهٔ بدهی ۳۰ سالهٔ دولت آمریکا.
us30y.ifRising: وام مسکن و وام‌های بلندمدت معمولاً گران‌تر می‌شوند.

connections.text: اوراق ۳۰ سالهٔ آمریکا بلندترین لنگر برای قیمت‌گذاری وام مسکن در آمریکاست.

fed-target.ifRising: وام‌ها و وام مسکن معمولاً گران‌تر می‌شوند و پس‌انداز بیشتر سود می‌دهد.
fed-target.ifFalling: وام‌ها و وام مسکن معمولاً ارزان‌تر می‌شوند و پس‌انداز کمتر سود می‌دهد.

connections.text: نرخ سیاستی انتهای کوتاه را پایه‌گذاری می‌کند؛ اوراق ۱۰ ساله انتظار بلندمدت را حمل می‌کند.

fed-target.australiaAngle: حرکات فدرال رزرو لحن نرخ‌های جهانی را تعیین می‌کند، از جمله مسیری که بانک مرکزی استرالیا می‌تواند با اعتبار طی کند.

ecb-dfr.oneLine: نرخی که بانک‌ها روی سپرده‌های خود در بانک مرکزی اروپا می‌گیرند.
ecb-dfr.ifRising: وام‌های منطقهٔ یورو معمولاً گران‌تر می‌شوند و پس‌انداز بیشتر سود می‌دهد.
ecb-dfr.ifFalling: وام‌های منطقهٔ یورو معمولاً ارزان‌تر می‌شوند و پس‌انداز کمتر سود می‌دهد.

connections.text: نرخ سپرده انتهای کوتاه منحنی منطقهٔ یورو را پایه‌گذاری می‌کند.

fed-expectations.oneLine: آنچه اوراق ۲ ساله دربارهٔ گام‌های بعدی فدرال رزرو نشان می‌دهد.
fed-expectations.ifRising: وقتی بازار نرخ بالاتر فدرال رزرو را قیمت‌گذاری می‌کند، وام‌برداری معمولاً پیش از حرکت بالا می‌رود.
fed-expectations.ifFalling: وقتی بازار نرخ پایین‌تر فدرال رزرو را قیمت‌گذاری می‌کند، وام‌برداری معمولاً پیش از حرکت آرام می‌شود.

connections.text: مسیر ضمنی از اوراق ۲ ساله، خوانش بازار از آنجا که فدرال رزرو می‌رود است.

govt-interest-revenue.oneLine: صرف‌شدن چه سهمی از درآمد دولت آمریکا به پرداخت بهرهٔ بدهی.
govt-interest-revenue.ifRising: سهم بیشتری از مالیات‌ها معمولاً صرف پرداخت بهره می‌شود و جدال بودجه‌ای آمریکا تندتر می‌شود.
govt-interest-revenue.ifFalling: سهم کوچک‌تر بهره معمولاً جای بیشتری برای هزینه‌های دیگر دولت باز می‌کند.

connections.text: نرخ‌های بلندمدت بالاتر معمولاً بهره‌ای را که دولت می‌پردازد با گذشت زمان بالا می‌برد.

us-2y.oneLine: نرخ بهرهٔ بدهی ۲ سالهٔ دولت آمریکا.
us-2y.ifRising: بازار معمولاً نرخ بالاتر فدرال رزرو را انتظار دارد و هزینهٔ وام کوتاه‌مدت اغلب بالا می‌رود.
us-2y.ifFalling: بازار معمولاً نرخ پایین‌تر فدرال رزرو را انتظار دارد و آسودگی زودتر به وام‌گیرندگان می‌رسد.
